final.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
final.body:
If you are weighing automation against another hire, don’t just ask what it costs to build. Ask what it costs to keep working when the model underneath it changes, gets retired, or becomes awkward to use.

That shows up in ordinary workflows: customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, invoice handling, or document sorting. On day one, the workflow can look fine. Later, a model change or pricing change may mean you need to adjust prompts, retest the flow, or fall back to manual work. That is not a catastrophe. It is a maintenance decision, and it belongs in the business case.

The practical next step is simple: before you approve a pilot, ask one blunt question. If the underlying model is upgraded, retired, or repriced, does this workflow keep running as designed, or do we need to rebuild parts of it and approve that spend again? If the answer is unclear, you do not have a complete plan yet.

Automation is easiest to justify when the workflow is stable and the owner understands the upkeep. Otherwise, the cheapest entry price can hide the harder part.

final.title: The quiet cost of model deprecation
final.body:
If you are comparing automation with another hire, the first cost is not the build. It is what happens later if the model underneath the workflow changes, gets retired, or becomes too awkward to keep using. That is the quiet cost: not a dramatic failure, just a workflow that may need attention again.

For a small business, this shows up in ordinary jobs like customer-inquiry triage, lead qualification, or invoice handling. A workflow can look fine on day one and still carry a maintenance question: if the model version shifts or the vendor changes pricing, does this still work, or do we need to rebuild and pay again?

That is a useful question to ask before you approve any automation pilot. It keeps the decision honest. Human approval still matters if the fix means spending more money, and the owner should know who owns the model-version call if a change happens later.

So the practical next step is simple: write down the recurring workflow, then ask whether it still works if the model is upgraded, retired, or repriced. If that answer is fuzzy, you do not have a finished plan yet — you have a hopeful sketch.
